item.question: Squares of areas 9 and 16 are to be combined into one square. What is its side?
steps: 3² = 9 and 4² = 16, so the sides are 3 and 4.
Put sides 3 and 4 at a right angle to make a right triangle.
By Verse 1.12 the square on its hypotenuse has area 9 + 16 = 25.
5² = 25, so the new square has side 5.
item.answer: Side 5: the hypotenuse of the right triangle with sides 3 and 4

item.question: Why are all four sides of the 4-sided figure T + U + V equal?
steps: T, U, W and X are all copies of the right triangle with perpendicular sides a and b.
Congruent triangles have equal hypotenuses.
Each side of the 4-sided figure is the hypotenuse of one of these triangles.
So all four sides have the same length, c.
item.answer: Each side is the hypotenuse of a congruent right triangle, so all four sides equal c

concept_name: Why does the square on the hypotenuse hold both squares exactly?

item.question: Explain Baudhāyana's assertion: the square on the hypotenuse has the same area as the two given squares.
steps: The square on the hypotenuse is made of T, U and V.
The two given squares, joined, are made of V, W and X.
T, U, W and X are congruent, so T and U together have the same area as W and X together.
So T + U + V has the same area as V + W + X.
Moving W and X to the places of T and U turns the two squares into the square on the hypotenuse.
item.answer: Square on the hypotenuse = T + U + V = V + W + X = the two given squares

concept_name: Four equal sides: why is every corner a right angle?

item.question: Explain why all the angles of this new 4-sided figure are right angles and so it is a square.
steps: In the right triangle with sides a and b, call one acute angle x; the angles add to 180 and one is 90, so the other acute angle is 90 − x.
At the corner on the bottom edge, the angle x of W and the angle 90 − x of X lie on the straight edge on either side of the corner, so the corner is 180 − x − (90 − x), which is 90.
At each of the other three corners, an angle x and an angle 90 − x together make the corner: x + (90 − x), which is 90.
Four equal sides and four right angles make a square.
item.answer: Every corner is a right angle and every side is c, so the figure is a square on the hypotenuse

concept_name: Two squares into one with paper: the theorem

item.question: Combine two squares of sides a and b using paper: make two cuts, get three pieces, and rearrange them into one square.
steps: Join the squares side by side along their bottoms, the square of side a on the left.
Mark the point on the bottom edge at distance a from the right end; it is b − a from the join.
Cut from that point to the top-left corner of the small square: this cut has length c.
Cut from the same point to the top-right corner of the large square: this cut also has length c.
Turn each right triangle a quarter turn about the outer top corner it shares with the squares: the three pieces make one square of side c.
item.answer: One square of side c, whose area is a² + b²

concept_name: What does Baudhāyana's theorem say, and why two names?

item.question: State Baudhāyana's theorem on right-angled triangles, and say why it has two names.
steps: Take a right triangle with shorter sides a and b.
The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, c.
The squares on a and b, cut and rearranged, exactly cover the square on c.
So a² + b² = c².
Baudhāyana (c. 800 BCE) stated it first in general form; Pythagoras (c. 500 BCE) studied it a couple of hundred years later.
item.answer: If a right-angled triangle has sides a, b and hypotenuse c, then a² + b² = c²

item.question: Using the constructions you have now seen, how would you construct a square whose area is triple the area of a given square? Five times the area of a given square? (Baudhāyana's Śulba-Sūtra, Verse 1.10)
steps_tex: Let the given square have side $a$ and area $a^2$.
Its diagonal $d$ is the side of the square with double the area: $d^2 = 2a^2$.
Make a right triangle with perpendicular sides $a$ and $d$.
The square on its hypotenuse has area $a^2 + 2a^2 = 3a^2$: triple.
For five times, make a right triangle with perpendicular sides $a$ and $2a$.
The square on its hypotenuse has area $a^2 + 4a^2 = 5a^2$.
item.answer_tex: Triple: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle whose sides are a side and a diagonal of the given square. Five times: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle with sides $a$ and $2a$
steps: Let the given square have side a and area a².
Its diagonal d is the side of the square with double the area: d² = 2a².
Make a right triangle with perpendicular sides a and d.
The square on its hypotenuse has area a² + 2a² = 3a²: triple.
For five times, make a right triangle with perpendicular sides a and 2a.
The square on its hypotenuse has area a² + 4a² = 5a².
item.answer: Triple: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle whose sides are a side and a diagonal of the given square. Five times: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle with sides a and 2a
item.text:

Answer: Triple: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle whose sides are a side and a diagonal of the given square. Five times: the square on the hypotenuse of the right triangle with sides $a$ and $2a$

concept_name: Add or subtract, and when the rule does not apply

item.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one side 5. Find the third side h.
steps: The side 5 and the side h meet at the right angle.
The side 13 is opposite the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse: c = 13.
The side h is at the right angle, so subtract.
item.text:
A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one side 5. Find the third side h.
1. The side 5 and the side h meet at the right angle.
2. The side 13 is opposite the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse: c = 13.
3. The side h is at the right angle, so subtract.
4. 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, so h² = 144.
5. 12² = 144, so h = 12.
Answer: 12 units

3. 14.4² = 207.36 and 14.5² = 210.25, so 14.4 < √208 < 14.5.
